The logic behind refusing a search without a warrant:

If the official is invited in, the property owner is misplacing his trust on that official based only upon what he "say's" he'll be looking for; that it will be the extent of his interest in the search. What really happens is that any plain or open view discoveries may be noted or gathered as evidence prior to an offense being prosecuted at a criminal level (at which point Miranda rights are explained). Misdemeanor or civil offenses can quickly be ascertained on this visit, even if the property owner has not expected it when permission was given. Observations from without the property line must always be described from that point of view.. so as to establish that the official both had the authority and the jurisdiction to use it as evidence.

A warrant clearly describes the scope of the search of the property, thereby limiting it to the items or reasons for the suspicion or cause. It keeps officials from conducting a full inquisition regarding the culpability of the subject of a search under such broad scope as to render a high probability of finding a violation of any laws or regulations within the officer's authority.

So, in short: It is almost never a good idea to let an official come aboard to "look around" the property based solely upon something less than their legal authority to do so without consent. Social calls are not their M.O.
